prize_parts.citation: For developing the political-economy theory of trade policy, showing how organised interests shape protection, and thereby linking trade theory to the analysis of political institutions.

statement.case_for: I keep B001 first after reading the openings. The Grossman-Helpman protection-for-sale framework turned lobbying and tariff formation into a tractable general-equilibrium model with testable implications. The model has been taken up in theory, in structural and reduced-form empirical work, and in the analysis of trade agreements. Attribution is the cleanest of any candidate: a long, tightly coupled two-person partnership, with the 1994 paper and the book on interest groups and trade policy as central outputs. Maturity is not a concern. The core results are three decades old and have been tested, criticised and extended. The prize would also recognise a contribution that connects trade, political economy and dynamic general-equilibrium modelling, which makes it relevant beyond one subfield. Several colleagues from different fields (Andersson, Enflo, Fredriksson, Friberg, Strömberg, Teorell) independently reached the same view on scientific grounds. I treat that agreement only as a sign that the attribution and maturity arguments hold up, not as merit in itself.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is empirical. Structural estimates of the protection-for-sale equilibrium are sensitive to specification, and direct support for its functional forms is mixed, so some of the contribution is a disciplined framework rather than a settled quantitative result. A second concern is thematic. Krugman's 2008 prize covered adjacent new trade theory, and the 2025 prize recognised innovation-driven growth, which could overlap with the Grossman-Helpman growth-and-trade strand if the citation leans on it. Helpman's credit on B030 also leaves open whether the committee prefers to reward trade through the firm-heterogeneity line.

responses.point: Krusell ranks the BLP demand-estimation and dynamic-industry-model work (B002) first. He argues that it changed empirical industrial organisation and is now routine in merger review, antitrust and regulation, and that Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes are a clear core.
responses.response: I accept that the practical reach and maturity of B002 are very high. I do not rank it above B001 for two reasons. The credited list has seven names and the three-name cap forces the exclusion of Bresnahan and Reiss, who made foundational contributions to empirical IO. Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes also reflect a methods contribution, and the committee would have to be comfortable rewarding a toolkit rather than a discovery about economic behaviour. B001's credit is cleaner. I would welcome a closer look at how much of B002's value lies in Pakes's dynamic-games work versus the BLP demand framework, because that would affect whether a three-person citation is stable.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B018 first. She argues that the task and skill-bias view of technology and the import-competition evidence changed understanding of wage inequality and local labour-market costs, and she would credit Autor, Hanson and Katz.
responses.response: I agree that the combination of credible research designs and a conceptual framework is a real strength, and I rank B018 fifth, not lower. My reservations are about attribution and persistence. The task framework has antecedents outside the credited names (Levy and Murnane), and Acemoglu's related theory is recognised through the 2024 prize. The long-run size and persistence of the China-shock effects are still being debated, and the Autor-Dorn-Hanson trade-shock work is a distinct strand from the Katz skill-premium work. Until the committee decides whether this is one discovery or two, I find B001's tighter attribution more defensible. I would not object to B018 as a later candidate once persistence evidence settles.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B001 first but notes that the citation must be drawn carefully. The trade-policy strand and the growth-and-trade strand are both joint work, and there may be overlap with the 2025 growth prize and earlier trade prizes.
responses.response: I agree, and the citation I propose is deliberately anchored on the stated discovery of B001, the political economy of trade policy and protection. The innovation and endogenous-growth strand is real joint work, but I would not make it the basis of the award. Doing so would invite overlap with the 2025 recognition of innovation-driven growth and make the citation harder to defend. I would also not ask the committee to settle Helpman's position on B030 first. The firm-heterogeneity contribution is a separate achievement, and a Grossman-Helpman award does not preclude later recognition of it.

responses.point: Boppart ranks the firm-heterogeneity candidate (B030) second, with Melitz as the central originator and Helpman as co-recipient, and he notes that Bernard, Eaton and Kortum are not credited.
responses.response: The firm-level selection framework is a distinct and influential advance, and I agree it is more than a refinement of Krugman's new trade theory. My concern is attribution. Melitz (2003) is a single central paper, and the exporter facts and early models of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are outside the credited names, as Boppart himself notes. That leaves a visible gap in any three-person citation. B001 has no comparable gap, which is why I rank it higher.

uncertainties: Whether the committee frames the award around trade-policy political economy alone or also credits the growth-and-trade strand, and how that interacts with the 2025 prize.
How much weight to give mixed empirical support for the protection-for-sale predictions relative to the framework's influence.
Whether recognising Helpman on B001 should be weighed against the separate firm-heterogeneity candidate B030.
For B036, whether the 2024 institutions prize makes the topic too close, and whether Besley belongs alongside Persson and Tabellini.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the preferred B001 laureates, Helpman and Grossman. My listed frequent co-authors (Krusell, Olovsson, Storesletten, Zilibotti, Rodríguez Mora) and committee co-authors (Boppart, Friberg) are not credited on B001. For the alternative B036, my opening noted a possible institutional link to Persson at IIES. The supplied profile does not document it, so I disclose it without adjudicating it.
